planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; single, golden-yellow spring flowers are typical of the species, but the real draw is the green cane striped lengthwise with bright yellow.

directions: Site this selection where its boldly striped bamboo-like canes can be admired in winter after leaf drop, ideally against a dark background such as an evergreen hedge. It suckers to form a colony over time and spreads more slowly than the double-flowered 'Pleniflora'. Thin out a portion of the oldest canes at ground level right after flowering each year, since old wood loses its cane coloration and blooms less freely than young growth. Give it morning sun for best stem color while protecting roots from prolonged drought.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in spring just below soil level in humus-rich, well-drained soil; this German-bred hybrid opens pure white flower clusters on red stems that age gracefully to soft pink as they mature.

directions: Silberlicht is one of the older and most garden-worthy Bergenia hybrids, holding a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for its reliable, clean white spring flower clusters that blush pink with age against handsome, rounded, leathery leaves. Foliage takes on bronze-red winter tones in cold weather, adding a second season of interest to the front of a shaded border. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in partial to full shade; it tolerates deeper shade than most flowering perennials. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in spring by cutting through the woody rhizomes.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring just below soil level in humus-rich, well-drained soil; this compact Bergenia hybrid produces deep magenta-crimson flower clusters and glossy leaves that turn rich purple-red through winter.

directions: Abendglut (Evening Glow) is a compact, slow-spreading Bergenia hybrid raised in Germany and grown for its saturated magenta-crimson flowers and unusually dark winter foliage color, which deepens to a rich beet-purple in cold weather more intensely than most Bergenia selections. Its smaller stature suits rock gardens, path edging, and container plantings where larger bergenias would overwhelm the space. Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist but well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and pull off tattered old leaves by hand each spring to keep the clump tidy. Divide the creeping rhizomes every four to five years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Braunlaub' (German for 'brown leaf') holds a strong bronze-brown cast in its deeply lobed, duck-foot-shaped leaves through much of the season.

directions: Braunlaub is a German-raised selection of Rodgersia podophylla valued for foliage that stays a rich coppery bronze from spring through summer, in contrast to seedling-grown plants of the species that often green up after their spring flush. Airy plumes of creamy-white to pale pink, astilbe-like flowers rise above the foliage in early to midsummer, followed by attractive reddish seed heads. Give it a sheltered, consistently moist site along a pond or stream margin, since the large, thin leaves scorch and tatter in wind or drought. Rich, humusy soil and dependable moisture keep the bronze color at its richest.

common_name: Denim 'n Lace Russian Sage (Extended-Bloom Compact Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this sterile hybrid selection begins blooming several weeks earlier than typical Russian sage and continues without setting seed, so it never becomes weedy in the garden.

directions: Denim 'n Lace is a sterile hybrid selection bred for a longer, earlier-starting bloom season than the straight species and a sturdier, more compact, self-supporting habit that resists flopping. Powder-blue flowers wreathe finely cut, silvery-gray, aromatic foliage from early summer well into fall, drawing bees and butterflies over an unusually long window. It was named a Perennial Plant Association Perennial Plant of the Year, reflecting its wide adaptability and low-maintenance performance. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun and cut the woody framework back hard in early spring as new basal growth emerges.

common_name: Silver Sheen Kohuhu (Silvery-Leaved New Zealand Pittosporum)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; near-black stems set off small, wavy-edged, silvery gray-green leaves on this New Zealand species, distinct from the broader, glossier foliage of Pittosporum tobira.

directions: Silver Sheen is one of the most widely grown selections of kohuhu, a New Zealand pittosporum species distinct from the more commonly grown Pittosporum tobira, valued for its slender, wavy, silvery-gray leaves held on nearly black young stems. Small, honey-scented, deep purple flowers appear inconspicuously in spring but perfume the air near the plant at dusk. It is faster growing and eventually larger than most tobira cultivars, tolerating shearing well as a screen or informal hedge, and its foliage is a favorite of florists for cut arrangements. Give it well-drained soil and full sun for the densest, most silvery growth, and provide wind shelter in the coldest part of its hardiness range.

common_name: Grand Bleu Bluebeard (Deep Blue Compact Caryopteris)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this French-bred selection is compact and exceptionally floriferous, wreathing its upper stems in intensely deep blue-violet flower clusters from late summer into fall.

directions: Grand Bleu was bred in France and selected for a tidy, rounded, compact habit paired with an unusually saturated deep blue flower color that holds up well in heat. Aromatic gray-green foliage covers the plant through summer before the dense clusters of fringed flowers open along the stem tips, providing valuable late-season nectar for bees and butterflies. Like other caryopteris, it dies back to the ground in cold winters and reliably resprouts from the base; cut the entire plant back to a few inches in late winter since flowers form on new growth. It thrives in poor to average, sharply drained soil and resents heavy, wet clay.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this UK-raised selection is grown chiefly for its crisp white-margined, gray-green variegated foliage, which brightens the border even before the pale blue flowers open in late summer.

directions: Snow Fairy was raised in England and holds a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for its striking cream-white leaf margins, which give the whole plant a frosted appearance from spring through fall, well before the light blue-violet flower clusters appear in late summer. It is slightly less vigorous than green-leaved caryopteris cultivars and benefits from full sun to keep the variegation crisp, since shade causes the pattern to fade toward plain green. Grow in poor to average, sharply drained soil, and cut the whole plant back hard to a few inches from the ground each late winter, since flowers and the best variegated new growth form on the current season's wood.

common_name: Mrs Popple Fuchsia (Hardy Scarlet-and-Violet Garden Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; one of the most widely planted hardy fuchsia cultivars, valued for its vigorous, floriferous habit and classic scarlet-and-violet bicolor blooms.

directions: Mrs Popple is a long-popular hardy fuchsia cultivar of Fuchsia magellanica parentage, bearing an abundance of medium-sized flowers with flared scarlet-red sepals over deep violet-purple corollas from early summer through fall. It has a bushier, more floriferous habit than the species and holds a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for garden performance. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; in cold winters it dies back to the ground and resprouts vigorously from the roots each spring, while in milder zones it remains semi-woody. Mulch heavily over the crown before winter in the coldest part of its range, and pinch young growth in spring to encourage a bushy, well-branched plant.

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in part shade; like other triphylla-type fuchsias, Thalia tolerates far more heat and direct sun than typical hybrid fuchsias and is damaged below 28F.

directions: Thalia is a long-established triphylla-type fuchsia hybrid, bred in the early twentieth century alongside 'Gartenmeister Bonstedt' and sharing its heat tolerance, velvety bronze-green foliage, and long, narrow, tubular flowers rather than the skirted bells of typical hybrid fuchsias. Clusters of intense orange-red flowers form at the branch tips from summer into fall and are a magnet for hummingbirds. It thrives in the heat and humidity that defeat many hybrid fuchsias, making it an excellent choice for a large container or summer bedding display in hot climates. Treat as an annual or overwinter cuttings indoors in zones below 10, and pinch young plants to encourage a fuller, more floriferous habit.

common_name: Sun Parasol Stars and Stripes Mandevilla (Pink-and-White Striped Trumpet Vine)
scientific_name: Mandevilla x amabilis 'Sun Parasol Stars and Stripes'

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed when soil and air are warm; this Sun Parasol series selection stands out for its pink flowers overlaid with irregular white streaks and blushes, no two blooms quite identical.

directions: Stars and Stripes is a novelty selection from the Sun Parasol mandevilla series prized for its large, funnel-shaped flowers in pink overlaid with variable white streaking, giving each bloom a hand-painted, candy-striped look. Like other Sun Parasol selections it twines vigorously and needs a trellis, fence, or pergola to climb, blooming continuously from late spring through frost on glossy, deep green foliage. Grow in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil, feeding every two weeks during the growing season for the strongest bloom show. In the warmest part of its range it may persist as a semi-woody perennial; elsewhere treat as an annual or bring container plants indoors before frost, and wear gloves when pruning since the milky sap can irritate skin.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; this Lemoine-bred selection bears large, star-shaped flowers in soft pink edged white, with a deeper rosy-purple reverse visible on the unopened buds.

directions: Magicien is a classic French Lemoine-bred Deutzia hybrid holding a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit, notable for its unusually large flowers among deutzias, borne in dense clusters along arching branches in late spring to early summer. Each bloom shows soft pink shading to white toward the petal edges, with the outer petal surface flushed a deeper mauve-pink visible from the bud stage onward, giving the shrub a two-toned effect in full bloom. Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil of average fertility, and prune immediately after flowering by removing a third of the oldest stems at ground level each year to keep the shrub vigorous and well-furnished with flowering wood.
